display.title: The Baal Shem Tov's L'chaim in the Forest
display.summary_short: Why we think before every brachah and eat only kosher food, and a Baal Shem Tov story about a mysterious meal in a forest that freed a wandering soul.
display.summary_long: The storyteller begins with Dovid HaMelech's words that the whole world belongs to Hashem, so a brachah is our way of asking permission before we eat. He tells how the Tzemach Tzedek taught a young Chassid to think 'To Whom am I saying Baruch Atah?' before every brachah, a story the Frierdiker Rebbe heard as a boy. Before the brachah comes checking that food is truly kosher, with a good hechsher and chalav Yisroel, and the Alter Rebbe's warning that non-kosher food weakens a person's emunah. Then the story: the Baal Shem Tov's horses stop deep in a forest, where he and ten students daven Mincha, eat a meal, pour a little mashkeh into the ground and say L'chaim. He explains with a story. A priest lured a young Torah scholar away from his family by secretly feeding him non-kosher meat, until he left Yiddishkeit. Years later, an old watchman, a hidden Jew from Spain weeping on Yom Kippur, awakened him to teshuvah. The old man set out on foot to live as a Jew and died in that very forest, and the students' mitzvos there brought his soul to Gan Eden.
display.lesson: Think about Hashem before every brachah, make sure what we eat is truly kosher, and know that a Jew can always do teshuvah.

advisories.note: A priest tricks a Torah scholar into eating non-kosher food and leaving Yiddishkeit; he later does teshuvah.
The scholar abandons his wife and children and marries the priest's daughter.
An old man dies alone in a forest on his way to live as a Jew.
Angels debate whether his soul may enter Gan Eden; it wanders until freed.

characters: Reb Dovid Tzvi (the Radatz), a Chassid

The Frierdiker Rebbe's account of the Radatz and the Tzemach Tzedek's instruction about brachos.
